1F OurBigBook.com
For a basis v1​,…,vd​ of the real vector space V, the Gram-Schmidt process constructs an orthonormal basis successively:
wj​=vj​−∑i<j​⟨vj​,ei​⟩ei​,ej​=⟨wj​,wj​⟩​wj​​.
(1)
The inner product makes wj​ orthogonal to all earlier ei​. Moreover wj​=0, since otherwise vj​ would be a linear combination of its predecessors, contrary to linear independence. Induction gives span(e1​,…,ej​)=span(v1​,…,vj​). Starting with a basis of a linear subspace U and extending it to a basis of V gives the same construction with the first r=dimU vectors spanning U.
The orthogonal complement is U⊥={v∈V:⟨v,u⟩=0 for every u∈U}. For every v∈V, set u=∑i=1r​⟨v,ei​⟩ei​. Then u∈U and v−u∈U⊥. If w∈U∩U⊥, then ⟨w,w⟩=0, so w=0 by definiteness of the inner product. Thus the direct sum is
V=U⊕U⊥​.
(2)
This also covers U=0 and U=V.
For the polynomial space, the form is immediately a symmetric bilinear form, and (f,f)=f(1)2+f(2)2+f(3)2≥0. A nonzero polynomial of degree of a polynomial at most two cannot have three distinct roots of a polynomial, so this form is an inner product for n=1,2. For n≥3, the nonzero polynomial (x−1)(x−2)(x−3) has (f,f)=0. Therefore, among the stipulated positive integers,
n∈{1,2}​.
(3)

Use the class equation for the action of G on itself by conjugation:
∣G∣=∣Z(G)∣+∑j​[G:CG​(gj​)],
(4)
where the sum runs over noncentral conjugacy classes. By Lagrange's theorem, each noncentral class has size a positive power of p greater than one. Thus ∣Z(G)∣≡∣G∣≡0(modp). Since the identity element belongs to the center of a group,
∣Z(G)∣≥p>1​.
(5)
For ∣G∣=p3, the possible orders of the center of a group are p,p2,p3. Order p3 would make G an abelian group. Order p2 would make the quotient group G/Z(G) have prime order and hence be a cyclic group. But a cyclic quotient by the center forces G to be Abelian: if gZ(G) generates the quotient, any two elements are gaz and gbw with z,w∈Z(G), and their products commute. Both larger orders contradict the hypothesis. Consequently
∣Z(G)∣=p​.
(6)

The chain rule for Fréchet derivatives states that if f is differentiable at a and g is differentiable at f(a), then
D(g∘f)a​=Dgf(a)​∘Dfa​​.
(7)
The composition on the right is a composition of linear maps, equivalently a product of Jacobian matrices in coordinates.
Apply the chain rule to the affine function x↦(x,c−x). The resulting derivative is
gc′​(x)=fx​(x,c−x)−fy​(x,c−x)​.
(8)
If the two partial derivatives agree everywhere, gc′​=0. The mean value theorem makes gc​ constant on R. Define h(c)=f(c,0), which is itself differentiable by the chain rule. Taking c=x+y gives gc​(x)=gc​(c)=h(c), and therefore
f(x,y)=h(x+y)​.
(9)
No continuity of the partial derivatives beyond the assumed differentiability is needed.

4F (Complex Analysis)

Words: 156 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 156
4F OurBigBook.com
Choose a star centre a of the open star-shaped set D and define the candidate antiderivative by a straight-segment contour integral:
F(z)=∫[a,z]​f(ζ)dζ.
(10)
For each fixed z∈D and all sufficiently small h, the filled triangle with vertices a,z,z+h lies in D. Indeed, the compact segment [a,z] has a neighbourhood of some positive radius contained in the open set D, and every point of this triangle lies within ∣h∣ of that segment. The zero triangle integral consequently gives
F(z+h)−F(z)=∫[z,z+h]​f(ζ)dζ=h∫01​f(z+th)dt.
(11)
By continuity, the last integral tends to f(z) as h→0. Hence
F′(z)=f(z)(z∈D)​.
(12)
In particular, this proves the existence of the antiderivative without incorrectly assuming the star-shaped set is convex.
On a general domain, the conclusion can fail. Take D=C∖{0} and f(z)=1/z. Every filled triangle contained in D has zero boundary integral by Cauchy integral theorem, but the unit circle has integral 2πi. An antiderivative would make every closed contour integral zero. This is the period obstruction to a holomorphic antiderivative: the local conclusion of Morera's theorem does not remove the global obstruction.

a OurBigBook.com
The wavefunction is a plane wave and a simultaneous formal eigenfunction of the momentum operator and the time-translation energy operator:
−iℏ∂x​ϕ=ℏkϕ,iℏ∂t​ϕ=Eϕ.
(19)
Its momentum and energy are therefore definite, while its probability density is spatially uniform:
p=ℏk,E=E,∣ϕ∣2=A2​.
(20)
For a particle of mass m, the probability current is j=(ℏ/m)Im(ϕ​∂x​ϕ)=ℏkA2/m, directed according to the sign of k.
On the whole real line, a nonzero constant-amplitude plane wave is not square-integrable and cannot be normalised to total probability one. It represents an idealised momentum eigenstate, interpreted through generalized eigenfunctions or as a limit of wave packets. Also, arbitrary k,E do not automatically solve the Schrödinger equation for a specified potential energy: for a free particle, E=ℏ2k2/(2m), or this value plus the constant potential energy for a constant-potential region. If A=0, the zero function is not a physical quantum state.

b

Words: 191 Articles: 1
6B OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 191
b OurBigBook.com
For a finite potential energy discontinuity, the stationary state ψ and its first derivative are continuous at a. Integrating the Time-independent Schrödinger equation across a shrinking interval about a gives continuity of ψ′; a jump in ψ would produce a distributional derivative incompatible with a finite potential energy.
For E>V0​, put k=2mE​/ℏ, q=2m(E−V0​)​/ℏ and use unit incident amplitude:
ψ(x)={eik(x−a)+re−ik(x−a),teiq(x−a),​x<a,x>a.​
(21)
There is no wave incident from the right. The matching equations 1+r=t, k(1−r)=qt give r=(k−q)/(k+q) and t=2k/(k+q). Comparing reflected and incident probability currents gives the reflection coefficient
R(E)=(E​+E−V0​​E​−E−V0​​​)2(E>V0​)​.
(22)
The transmitted fraction is T=(q/k)∣t∣2=4kq/(k+q)2, so R+T=1.
For 0<E<V0​, write κ=2m(V0​−E)​/ℏ and retain only the decaying right-hand solution te−κ(x−a). Matching gives r=(k−iκ)/(k+iκ), which has modulus one. The evanescent wave carries no transmitted probability current. At E=V0​, the bounded right-hand solution is constant and matching again gives r=1. Thus
R(E)=1(0<E≤V0​)​.
(23)
Classically, a particle is wholly transmitted for E>V0​ and wholly reflected for E<V0​; there is no classical partial reflection above the step. At the threshold it has zero right-hand speed and no transmitted flux, a marginal case requiring a convention about motion exactly on the discontinuity. The quantum result approaches R=0 as E/V0​→∞.

A(r)=4πμ0​I​∮C​∣r−r′∣dr′​,∣r−r′∣1​=r1​+r3r⋅r′​+O(r−3),

with the loop held fixed as r=∣r∣→∞. The first term integrates to zero since C is closed. Define its oriented vector area by
S=21​∮C​r′×dr′=∫Σ​ndS.
(25)
The second equality is Stokes theorem, applied componentwise to any oriented spanning surface. In particular the vector area is independent of the choice of spanning surface. From ∮C​d(ri′​rj′​)=0, the matrix ∮C​ri′​drj′​ is antisymmetric, which gives ∮C​(r⋅r′)dr′=S×r. Hence
m=IS,A(r)=4πμ0​​r3m×r​+O(r−3)​.

The orientation follows the current by the right-hand rule. For r=0, taking the curl of this leading magnetic vector potential gives the magnetic dipole field

For a planar loop, S is the signed area times the unit normal vector. For a nonplanar loop it is the oriented vector area, rather than the scalar area of an arbitrarily chosen surface.

9H OurBigBook.com
Let S0​=0 and let each increment of the simple symmetric random walk be uniformly chosen from {±e1​,±e2​,±e3​}. A return requires an even number of steps. In 2n steps returning to zero, let a,b,c be the respective numbers of positive steps in the three directions; there must also be a,b,c negative steps, so a+b+c=n. Counting step sequences gives
u2n​:=P0​(S2n​=0)=62n(2n)!​∑a+b+c=n​a!2b!2c!21​=4n(n2n​)​∑a+b+c=n​(3na!b!c!n!​)2.
(31)
The terms pabc​=n!/(3na!b!c!) form a multinomial distribution, so ∑pabc2​≤(maxpabc​)∑pabc​=maxpabc​. The permitted combinatorial inequalities give (n2n​)/4n≤C1​n−1/2 and maxa+b+c=n​pabc​≤C2​/n for n≥1. The second bound also follows by noting that the largest multinomial coefficient occurs when a,b,c differ by at most one and then applying Stirling formula. Thus
u2n​≤Cn−3/2,u2n+1​=0,j≥0∑​P0​(Sj​=0)<∞​.
(32)
To prove the origin is a transient state, let q be the probability of at least one return after time zero. The Strong Markov property at successive returns gives P(N≥k)=qk for the number N of later returns. Therefore E(N+1)=∑j​uj​ would be infinite if q=1. The bound forces q<1, proving that the origin is a transient state. Translation invariance gives the same conclusion at every lattice point. The coordinate walks need not be treated as independent; the counting via multinomial coefficients already incorporates their dependence.

The dual space here is the algebraic dual space X∗=HomR​(X,R), consisting of every linear functional; no topology or boundedness is imposed. For a basis e1​,…,en​, define ei∗​(∑j​xj​ej​)=xi​. These are linear functionals satisfying ei∗​(ej​)=δij​. Evaluating ∑i​ai​ei∗​=0 on each ej​ gives aj​=0, proving linear independence. Conversely, for every T∈X∗,
T=∑i=1n​T(ei​)ei∗​.
(33)
This proves spanning and hence proves, without assuming a dimension theorem, that the dual basis is a basis and dimX∗=n.
The canonical bidual evaluation map is
J:X⟶X∗∗,J(x)(T)=T(x)​.
(34)
Its definition makes no choice of basis and it is linear. If x=0, one coordinate functional is nonzero on x, so J is injective. For any B∈X∗∗, choose x=∑i​B(ei∗​)ei​. Expanding T in the dual basis gives T(x)=∑i​T(ei​)B(ei∗​)=B(T), proving surjection explicitly. Thus J is an isomorphism.
If T1​,…,Tn​ is any basis of X∗, its dual basis B1​,…,Bn​ in X∗∗ exists by the result just proved. Put vj​=J−1(Bj​). These vectors form a basis of X, and Ti​(vj​)=Bj​(Ti​)=δij​. Every basis of the finite-dimensional dual is a dual basis, of a uniquely determined basis of X.
For a separating subspace of an algebraic dual W, choose a basis T1​,…,Tr​ of W. The linear map x↦(T1​(x),…,Tr​(x)) is injective because W separates nonzero vectors. The rank-nullity theorem implies n≤r; but W⊆X∗ implies r≤n. Hence
W=X∗​.
(35)
The zero-dimensional case also has this conclusion.
For X=R[x], the monomials 1,x,x2,… form an infinite basis, each polynomial using only finitely many of them. The map T↦(T(1),T(x),T(x2),…) identifies X∗ with all real sequences, because any sequence (aj​) defines T(∑j=0d​cj​xj)=∑j=0d​cj​aj​. The linear subspace of finitely supported sequences is proper (it excludes (1,1,…)) and separating (one coefficient functional detects any nonzero polynomial). Thus
R(N0​)⊊RN0​≅X∗ is separating​.
(36)

a OurBigBook.com
The structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain applies in particular to a Euclidean domain R: every finitely generated module has an isomorphism
M≅Rr⊕R/(d1​)⊕⋯⊕R/(dk​),d1​∣d2​∣⋯∣dk​,
(37)
with each di​ nonzero and a nonunit. The rank of a free module r and the invariant factors of a finitely generated module di​ are unique up to multiplication by units; empty sums are allowed. This is the classification theorem being used, without a proof of that theorem.
The rational canonical form theorem states that for a linear operator T on a finite-dimensional vector space over any field F, there are unique monic nonconstant polynomials p1​∣⋯∣pk​ such that some basis gives
[T]=diag(C(p1​),…,C(pk​))​.
(38)
Here, for p(t)=td+ad−1​td−1+⋯+a0​, the companion matrix has ones on its subdiagonal and last column (−a0​,…,−ad−1​)T. The empty matrix covers a zero-dimensional space. Two linear operators have matrix similarity exactly when they have the same invariant factors of a linear operator.
For the proof, make V an F[t]-module by t⋅v=T(v). It is a finitely generated module, since a vector-space basis also generates it as a module. It is a torsion module: the powers of T have linear dependence in the finite-dimensional space EndF​(V), so some nonzero polynomial annihilates every vector. Because F[t] is a Euclidean domain, the classification theorem gives
V≅⨁i=1k​F[t]/(pi​),p1​∣⋯∣pk​.
(39)
There is no free summand, since a nonzero free module over F[t] is not a torsion module. Choose monic generators of the ideals. On F[t]/(pi​), the classes of 1,t,…,tdi​−1 form an F-basis by polynomial division. Multiplication by t is exactly C(pi​) in that basis, proving existence. Uniqueness in the classification theorem proves uniqueness of the rational canonical form. Finally, an F[t]-module isomorphism is precisely an invertible F-linear map intertwining the operators, establishing the assertion about matrix similarity. In particular the characteristic polynomial is ∏i​pi​ and the minimal polynomial is pk​ for nonzero V.

b OurBigBook.com
Induct on n to prove the stronger assertion that any submodule M⊆Rn is a free module of rank of a free module at most n. For n=0 this is immediate. Project onto the first coordinate by π:Rn→R. Its image π(M) is an ideal of the principal ideal domain, so π(M)=(a).
If a=0, then M embeds in the remaining n−1 coordinates and the induction hypothesis applies. Otherwise choose v∈M with π(v)=a. Put N=M∩kerπ, a submodule of Rn−1, which is free by induction. For every m∈M, there is b∈R with π(m)=ba, so m−bv∈N. If bv∈N, then ba=0; the integral domain property and a=0 give b=0. Therefore
M=Rv⊕N≅R⊕N​.
(40)
Appending v to a basis of N proves that M is a free module of rank of a free module at most n. This proof of the submodule theorem for free modules over a principal ideal domain does not assume in advance that M is a finitely generated module.

A function f:U→Rn has a Fréchet derivative at a∈U if there is a linear map A:Rm→Rn such that
f(a+h)=f(a)+Ah+o(∥h∥)(h→0)​.
(41)
The remainder condition is a limit in all directions at once, not merely the existence of partial derivatives.
For the stated scalar two-variable result, fix a=(a1​,a2​) and choose a small rectangle contained in the open set U. Split the increment into two coordinate segments. Applying the one-dimensional mean value theorem on each segment yields
f(a1​+h,a2​+k)−f(a)=hfx​(a1​+θh,a2​+k)+kfy​(a1​,a2​+σk)
(42)
for θ,σ∈(0,1), omitting a term if its increment is zero. Subtract hfx​(a)+kfy​(a). By continuity of the partial derivatives, for any ε>0 the remainder has modulus at most ε(∣h∣+∣k∣)≤2​εh2+k2​ for sufficiently small increments. This proves differentiability, with Jacobian matrix (fx​(a),fy​(a)).
Away from the origin the specified rational function has a nonzero denominator and is smooth. At the origin, f(t,0)=t and f(0,t)=2t2, so the partial derivatives are fx​(0,0)=1, fy​(0,0)=0. Any Fréchet derivative there would therefore be A(h,k)=h. However,
f(t,t)=2t​+t2,2​∣t∣∣f(t,t)−t∣​⟶22​1​=0.
(43)
Thus
f is differentiable exactly on R2∖{(0,0)}​.
(44)
The failure is not merely a failure of continuity: ∣f(x,y)∣≤∣x∣+2y2→0 at the origin, so the function is continuous there.

a OurBigBook.com
Let {Oi​} be an open cover of Z in its subspace topology. Write Oi​=Z∩Ui​ with each Ui​ open in X. Since Z is a closed set, X∖Z is open, and {Ui​}∪{X∖Z} is an open cover of the compact space X. A finite subcover restricts to a finite subcover of Z. Hence the closed subset Z is compact.
If {Vj​} is an open cover of f(Z) in its subspace topology, the inverse images under the restricted continuous map f∣Z​ form an open cover of Z. Take a finite subcover; the corresponding Vj​ cover f(Z). Thus the continuous image f(Z) is compact. Neither argument assumes a Hausdorff space or asserts that a compact set must be closed set in an arbitrary topological space.

The labels (i) and (ii) in the original PDF are hypotheses of one theorem, not separate requests. Here is the finite-cover step furnished by the compact fibres. Start with any open cover {Ui​}i∈I​ of f−1(K), with the Ui​ open in X (a relative cover can be lifted to one of this form). For each y∈K, compactness gives a finite set Iy​⊆I with
f−1({y})⊆Vy​:=⋃i∈Iy​​Ui​.
(45)
An empty fibre needs no cover elements: take Iy​=∅ and Vy​=∅.
The complementary set Ay​=X∖Vy​ is closed set. By the closed map hypothesis, its image is closed set, so
Wy​:=Y∖f(Ay​)
(46)
is open, contains y, and satisfies f−1(Wy​)⊆Vy​. These open sets cover the compact set K. Select finitely many, Wy1​​,…,Wym​​. The finitely many original cover elements with indices in Iy1​​∪⋯∪Iym​​ then cover f−1(K). Therefore
f−1(K) is compact​.
(47)
This proves the unheaded conclusion in the PDF as well as explaining the role of hypothesis (i). No Hausdorff assumption is needed for this compact-preimage theorem for closed maps.

W=Y∖f(X∖V) open,y∈W,f−1(W)⊆V​.

Applying this to the finite union covering each compact fibre supplies a whole neighbourhood of that fibre's value using the same finitely many cover elements. Compactness of K selects finitely many such neighbourhoods and hence a finite subcover of f−1(K), proving the desired compact-preimage theorem for closed maps.
The closed map assumption cannot simply be omitted. Give X={0,1,2,…} the discrete topology and Y={0}∪{1/n:n≥1} the usual subspace topology from R. The bijection f(0)=0, f(n)=1/n is continuous, and all its fibres are compact singletons. But Y is compact whereas f−1(Y)=X is an infinite discrete space, which is not compact. The map is not closed set, since the closed subset {1,2,…} has image {1,1/2,…}, missing its limit point 0.

ξ=sin(x/4)cosh(y/4),η=cos(x/4)sinh(y/4).

Injectivity follows from the identities for equal sines: the alternatives z1​/4=z2​/4+2πn and z1​/4=π−z2​/4+2πn give only the identical point within this strip. Surjectivity can be seen directly: for fixed ξ and v=y/4>0, solve sin(x/4)=ξ/coshv; then
η2=sinh2v−ξ2tanh2v.

On v>max(0,arcosh∣ξ∣), with the lower endpoint read as 0 when ∣ξ∣≤1, the right side increases strictly from zero to infinity. Thus every point of the upper half-plane has a unique preimage.
By conformal invariance of harmonicity, write the transformed harmonic function as Φ(ξ,η). Its real-axis boundary data are
F(s)={f(4arcsins),0,​−1<s<1,∣s∣>1.​​

2π1​∫R​eiku−∣k∣ηdk=π(η2+u2)η​.

ϕ(x,y)=Φ(ξ,η)=πη​∫−11​η2+(ξ−s)2F(s)​ds​.

There is no solution continuous on the entire closed half-strip for these data: the bottom edge has corner limits ±1, but the side edges have corner limits zero. 15G OurBigBook.com
Use curvature −1. In the Poincare disc model, hyperbolic lines are Euclidean diameters and arcs of circles orthogonal to the unit circle, with hyperbolic length element ds=2∣dz∣/(1−∣z∣2). In the upper half-plane model, they are vertical lines and semicircles with centres on the real axis, with ds=∣dz∣/Imz. Both displayed hyperbolic metrics are positive scalar multiples of the Euclidean metric, so their angles agree with Euclidean angles. The hyperbolic distance is the length of the joining hyperbolic line segment; explicitly, in the upper half-plane model,
d(P,Q)=arcosh(1+2ImPImQ∣P−Q∣2​)​.
(55)
In the Poincare disc model it is 2artanh∣(P−Q)/(1−PQ)∣.
For distinct P,Q, a isometry sends their joining hyperbolic line to the imaginary axis, so their images are ip,iq with p,q>0. For any continuously differentiable curve x(t)+iy(t) joining them,
ℓ(γ)=∫y(t)x′(t)2+y′(t)2​​dt≥∫y(t)∣y′(t)∣​dt≥∣logq−logp∣=d(P,Q).
(56)
Equality in the first inequality requires x′=0 everywhere, because the nonnegative difference is continuous. Equality in the second requires y′ to have one sign, allowing zero intervals. Thus equality holds precisely for a monotone reparametrisation of the joining hyperbolic segment. Conversely every such reparametrisation gives equality. For P=Q, equality means length zero and the constant curve; monotonicity is understood non-strictly.
Two distinct hyperbolic lines are parallel hyperbolic lines if they are disjoint in the plane and have exactly one common ideal endpoint; they are ultraparallel hyperbolic lines if they are disjoint and have no common ideal endpoint. To prove the common perpendicular of ultraparallel hyperbolic lines theorem, send one line to the imaginary axis. An ultraparallel hyperbolic lines second line can, after reflection if necessary, be written as a semicircle with centre c>0 and radius r satisfying c>r. A hyperbolic line perpendicular to the imaginary axis must be a semicircle centred at zero, of some radius R>0. The Euclidean condition for its orthogonality to the second circle is
R2=c2−r2​.
(57)
This has exactly one positive solution, proving existence and uniqueness. Conversely, if such a common perpendicular exists, the second line cannot be another vertical line, and the same condition forces ∣c∣>r, so its endpoints lie strictly on one side of zero and it is ultraparallel hyperbolic lines. This includes exclusion of intersecting lines (∣c∣<r) and parallel hyperbolic lines (∣c∣=r or another vertical line). The statement concerns distinct lines: a line coincident with itself would have many perpendiculars.
A horocycle in the upper half-plane model is either a Euclidean circle tangent to the real axis from above, with the tangent point as its ideal centre of a horocycle, or a horizontal line y=h>0, whose ideal centre of a horocycle is infinity. A isometry sending this centre to infinity sends the horocycle to a horizontal line. The hyperbolic lines meeting that horizontal line orthogonally are exactly the vertical lines; therefore the hyperbolic lines orthogonal to a horocycle are exactly those with its ideal centre as an endpoint.
If two horocycles have distinct horocycle centres, the unique hyperbolic line with those two ideal endpoints meets both orthogonally. If they have the same horocycle centre, send it to infinity: both become horizontal lines and every vertical hyperbolic line meets both orthogonally. Hence
The common orthogonal line is unique exactly when the ideal centres differ.​
(58)
In the other case there are infinitely many; intersection or tangency of the two horocycles does not change this classification.

Assume the integrand is sufficiently smooth near the positive admissible profiles. Define the second variation as δ2F[y,ξ]=d2F[y+εξ]/dε2​ε=0​, so it is twice the quadratic Taylor coefficient. Differentiation under the integral gives
δ2F=∫αβ​(fyy​ξ2+2fyp​ξξ′+fpp​ξ′2)dx,p=y′.
(59)
Integrating the middle term by parts, with ξ(α)=ξ(β)=0, yields
δ2F=∫αβ​[(fyy​−dxd​fyp​)ξ2+fpp​ξ′2]dx​.
(60)
All coefficients are evaluated along y.
For the surface-area integrand f=2πy1+p2​, the Beltrami identity for a stationary profile reads
f−pfp​=1+y′2​2πy​=2πE.
(61)
Equivalently, its Euler-Lagrange equation is yy′′=1+y′2, solved by the positive catenoid profile y=Ecosh((x−x0​)/E) with E>0. Equal boundary radii at x=±L, for L>0, require x0​=0, so
y(x)=Ecosh(x/E),a=Ecosh(L/E)​.
(62)
Direct substitution also verifies the Euler-Lagrange equation. This is a stationary profile whenever a positive E satisfying the boundary relation exists; such an E does not exist for arbitrary ring separations and radii.
On this profile, with z=x/E, the coefficients are fyy​=0, fpp​=2πEsech2z and dfyp​/dx=(2π/E)sech2z. Changing variables therefore gives
δ2F=2π∫−L/EL/E​(ξz2​−ξ2)sech2zdz​.
(63)
The printed strict inequality must mean every nonzero admissible variation: the zero function makes the integral zero, so the literal quantifier including it is false.
For completeness, the strict positivity here is sufficient for a strict local minimum in the fixed-endpoint C1 topology, among positive axisymmetric graph profiles. On this finite interval the weight p(z)=sech2z has a positive minimum. The regular Sturm-Liouville problem associated with Q[ξ]=∫p(ξz2​−ξ2) has an attained lowest Dirichlet eigenvalue λ1​ in the Rayleigh quotient. Its first eigenfunction is a nonzero smooth admissible variation; the assumed strict positivity gives λ1​>0. Hence Q≥λ1​∥ξ∥L22​. Combining this with Q≥pmin​∥ξz​∥L22​−pmax​∥ξ∥L22​ proves coercivity in the Sobolev space H01​.
The coefficients of the second variation depend continuously on (y,y′) while y>0. For a sufficiently small C1 perturbation, the quadratic forms along the segment from the stationary profile to the perturbed one retain a uniform positive coercivity bound. Taylor's formula with integral remainder, and the vanishing first variation, then gives F[y+v]−F[y]≥c∥v∥H12​>0 for nonzero sufficiently small admissible v. The stationary area is therefore a strict local minimum under the stated nonzero-variation condition. This supplies the uniform bound needed in an infinite-dimensional problem, rather than relying on pointwise positivity alone in an arbitrary function space.

Take K>0. For t>0, the diffusion fundamental solution of a linear differential operator F satisfies (∂t​−K∂x2​)F=0 and has initial value δ(x) in the sense of distributions:
t↓0lim​∫R​F(x,t)ψ(x)dx=ψ(0)​
(64)
for every smooth compactly supported test function ψ. With the usual spatial decay it has unit mass. Equivalently the causal extension Θ(t)F(x,t) is a retarded fundamental solution satisfying (∂t​−K∂x2​)(ΘF)=δ(x)δ(t).
The causal Green function is zero for t<τ and satisfies
(∂t​−K∂x2​)G(x,t;y,τ)=δ(x−y)δ(t−τ)​.
(65)
For t>τ it solves the homogeneous diffusion equation, and its initial jump is G(x,τ+;y,τ)=δ(x−y), again distributionally. The natural spatial decay and a standard bounded or integrable solution class specify the usual kernel, avoiding unrestricted growing solutions. The PDE acts on x,t; y,τ label the location and time of the unit impulse. Values of the Heaviside step function exactly at the jump do not affect these distribution identities.

vτ​(x,t)=∫R​F(x−y,t−τ)h(y,τ)dy(t>τ).

ϕ(x,t)=∫0t​vτ​(x,t)dτ=∫0t​∫R​F(x−y,t−τ)h(y,τ)dydτ​.

Physically, each short time interval adds h(⋅,τ)dτ to the temperature profile; that addition subsequently undergoes homogeneous diffusion equation. qt​=ζt​−h0​f​ηt​=0,Qt​=0​.

The two even branches approach ±c∣k∣ at large ∣k∣ and have values ±∣f∣ at k=0. The original dispersion diagram below also compares the speed magnitudes.
For k=0, the phase velocity and group velocity magnitudes are
∣cp​∣=∣k∣∣ω∣​=c2+k2f2​​,∣cg​∣=​dkdω​​=f2+c2k2​c2∣k∣​,∣cp​∣∣cg​∣=c2​.

For f=0, longer wavelengths have greater phase velocity but smaller group velocity: individual crests and wave packets therefore answer “faster or slower” differently. At long wavelength, ∣k∣≪∣f∣/c, the frequency is nearly the inertial frequency ∣f∣, ∣cp​∣∼∣f∣/∣k∣, and ∣cg​∣∼c2∣k∣/∣f∣. Rotation has its largest relative effect here, and the waves are strongly dispersive. At short wavelength, ∣k∣≫∣f∣/c, both speeds tend to c and rotation gives only a small, weakly dispersive correction. If f=0, the gravity waves are nondispersive, with speed c; at k=0 the phase velocity formula is undefined.

a OurBigBook.com
Let P0​,P1​ be simple hypotheses with densities p0​,p1​ (their Radon-Nikodym derivatives) relative to a common dominating measure. A possibly randomised statistical test is a measurable function φ∈[0,1]; its size of a statistical test is E0​φ and its statistical power is E1​φ. The Neyman-Pearson lemma says that a likelihood ratio threshold test
φ∗​(x)=⎩⎨⎧​1,0,γ(x),​p1​(x)>cp0​(x),p1​(x)<cp0​(x),p1​(x)=cp0​(x),​c≥0,
(76)
chosen to have size α, is a most powerful test among tests of size at most α. A constant randomisation on the equality set suffices to reach the required size; sets where p0​=0<p1​ are always rejected. For 0<α<1, a quantile of the likelihood ratio under P0​ gives such a threshold. If the threshold is zero, randomisation where p1​=0 may be needed to use the remaining size. At α=0, one can reject only a P0​-null set and optimally reject the part supporting P1​; at α=1, always reject.
For the proof, every competing φ satisfies
(φ∗​−φ)(p1​−cp0​)≥0
(77)
pointwise: the signs agree off the equality set, where the product is zero. Integrating gives
E1​φ∗​−E1​φ≥c(E0​φ∗​−E0​φ)≥0.
(78)
Thus the likelihood-ratio threshold test has maximum power at the stated level. If c>0, a competing most-powerful test must have size α and agree with φ∗​ off the equality set, apart from sets null for P0​+P1​; both inequalities must then be equalities. For c=0, equal size is not necessary for optimality, because changing decisions where p1​=0 does not affect power. These qualifications account for ties and singular supports rather than assuming all densities are strictly positive.

Under the null hypothesis θ=0, X has the uniform distribution on [0,1]. Against θ=1, the likelihood ratio is 2x, increasing on that interval. The Neyman-Pearson lemma therefore gives
Reject H0​ when X>1−α(0≤α≤1)​.
(79)
The size of a statistical test is P0​(X>1−α)=α, and there is no boundary randomisation issue for this continuous probability distribution. Its statistical power against θ=1 is ∫1−α1​2xdx=2α−α2.
For every admissible alternative 0<θ≤1, the likelihood ratio 1−θ+2θx is strictly increasing. The same upper-tail rejection set has size α and is a most powerful test against each fixed such alternative, again by the Neyman-Pearson lemma. Hence the same test is a uniformly most powerful test against θ>0, where the alternative is understood within the specified parameter range. Its full power function is
β(θ)=∫1−α1​(1−θ+2θx)dx=α+θα(1−α)​.

For α=0 or 1, the never-reject or always-reject test supplies the respective endpoint case.

A finite flow network is a directed graph with distinguished source s, sink t, and nonnegative finite flow network edge capacities cij​ on its directed edges. A feasible flow consists of numbers fij​ satisfying
0≤fij​≤cij​,∑j​fij​=∑j​fji​(i=s,t).
(81)
The second condition is flow conservation; absent edges contribute zero. The strength of a flow is its net outflow from the source,
∣f∣=∑j​fsj​−∑j​fjs​,
(82)
which equals net inflow to the sink by summing flow conservation over the other vertices. The maximum flow problem is
maximise ∣f∣ over all feasible flows​.
(83)
No assumption that a capacity-saturating flow at the source is feasible downstream is made. On a finite network a maximum exists, because the constraints define a nonempty compact set of edge flows and the objective is continuous.

b OurBigBook.com
The Ford-Fulkerson algorithm starts with zero flow. For each original edge i→j, the residual network has a forward edge with residual capacity cij​−fij​ and a reverse edge with residual capacity fij​. Distinguish these labelled residual edges if the original graph has antiparallel edges. While there is a source-to-sink augmenting path with positive residual capacities, increase the flow by the minimum residual capacity along it, adding on forward edges and subtracting on reverse edges. This preserves capacity bounds and flow conservation and increases the strength of a flow by that positive bottleneck.
A cut of a flow network is a partition (S,V∖S) with s∈S, t∈/S, of capacity c(S)=∑i∈S,j∈/S​cij​. Summing flow conservation gives ∣f∣=f(S,V∖S)−f(V∖S,S)≤c(S). The max-flow min-cut theorem states
fmax​∣f∣=S:s∈S,t∈/Smin​c(S)​.
(84)
When no augmenting path remains, take S to be the vertices reachable from s in the residual network. Every original outgoing edge of this cut of a flow network is saturated and every incoming edge has zero flow; otherwise a positive residual edge would leave S. Thus ∣f∣=c(S), certifying optimality and the theorem. For general finite real capacities, one can also apply this argument to an existing maximum: it cannot admit an augmenting path.
With integer capacities, each augmentation increases the value by at least one, so the Ford-Fulkerson algorithm terminates. Rational capacities can be scaled to integers. Arbitrary path choices with irrational capacities need not terminate; the existence theorem does not justify claiming finite termination in that generality. The given network has integer capacities, so this caveat does not obstruct its computation.

No: the increase need not equal ε. For a simple counterexample, use two edge-disjoint paths s→a→t and s→b→t, with all four capacities equal to one. Initially the maximum flow is 2. After every capacity increases to 1+ε, send 1+ε down each path; a source cut of a flow network bounds the total by the same value. Hence
new maximum=2+2ε,increase=2ε​.
(87)
More generally, by the max-flow min-cut theorem, if m(S) is the number of directed edges leaving a cut of a flow network, uniform capacity perturbation of a flow network gives
v(ε)=S:s∈S,t∈/Smin​(c(S)+εm(S))​.
(88)
The number of outgoing edges, and possible changes of the minimising cut of a flow network, determine the increase. If the question were interpreted as asking for an increase of at least ε, this does hold when the graph has a directed s-to-t path, because then every cut of a flow network has m(S)≥1. Without such a path a zero-edge cut of a flow network remains of capacity zero and the maximum can stay zero. Thus neither an exact increment nor an unconditional positive increment follows merely by adding the same amount to every edge capacity.
